title: Rerum Novarum (1891)
hook: Leo XIII writes on workers: fair wages, unions and dignity

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Bosco and the boys of Turin. Your line was reason, faith, kindness. Today, a pope writes about the factory floor.

A factory whistle before sunrise. Men, women and children walk in through the gate, and they will not walk out until dark. The pay barely covers bread and rent. If someone is hurt at the machine, there is often no help and no job tomorrow. In the cities of the new industrial age, people argued hard about what to do. Some said the owners owed nothing beyond the agreed wage. Others said the whole system should be torn down. Then a pope, Leo the Thirteenth, sent a letter to the bishops of the world, and it was about workers.
screen: `A FACTORY WHISTLE BEFORE DAWN.` → `TWO LOUD ANSWERS.` → `A POPE WRITES ABOUT WORKERS.`

segments.voice: Papal letters like this are called encyclicals, named for their first words in Latin. This one begins Rerum novarum, of new things. In Latin the phrase also meant upheaval, even revolution, and the letter opens on that restless spirit of change: new industries, great wealth for a few, a new kind of poverty for many. Leo makes four arguments. First, the worker is a person. Employers must not treat workers as slaves or as tools, and must respect their dignity as human beings. Second, a just wage. An agreement about pay is not automatically fair just because both sides signed it. A wage must be enough to support a worker who lives simply and works honestly. If hunger forces a man to accept less, that is injustice, even if it is a contract. Jesus says it plainly in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "for the labourer is worthy of his hire." Third, unions. Leo defends the right of workers to form associations, to band together for their own good. Fourth, no class war. Leo also defends private property, and rejects the idea that owners and workers are natural enemies. Each has duties to the other, he says, and the state has a duty to protect the weakest. That gives today's word, social teaching: the body of the Church's teaching about how a society should be ordered, on work, wages, property, the poor, the common good. Later popes kept returning to Rerum Novarum and building on it. Leo's answer, in the end, was that the person at the machine matters more than the machine.
screen: `RERUM NOVARUM: OF NEW THINGS.` · `NOT A TOOL. A PERSON.` · `A WAGE YOU CAN LIVE ON.` · `UNIONS, AND NO CLASS WAR.` · then, large: `WORTHY OF HIS HIRE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day: whose work touched your life? The person who stocked the shelves, drove the bus, cleaned the office, cooked the food; pick one, and if you know their name, say it quietly to yourself. If you pray, pray for them and their family; if you don't, hold them with respect.
Social teaching. The Catholic Church's teaching on how society should be ordered, on work, wages, property and the common good. Rerum Novarum is a key letter in it.
Your line: the dignity of work. A worker is a person, never just a tool. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes, schools and charities draw on the Church's social teaching in their work for fair wages, housing and the poor, and on May 1 the Church keeps the memorial of Saint Joseph the Worker.

chat.says: If a worker agrees to a wage, isn't that automatically fair?
options: Not for Leo XIII: a wage must be enough to live on, or it's unjust even if signed.
Yes for Leo XIII: any wage both sides sign is just, since they agreed freely.
Not for Leo XIII: he said private property and wages should be abolished.
chat.meaning: Leo argued pay isn't fair just because both sides signed: a wage must support a worker who lives simply and works honestly.
